You are picking up Task 9 at fix round 3. A prior implementer completed rounds 1 and 2 and then stalled at the start of round 3 — you own it now.

Work from: `/Users/akamaotto/code/icubefarm/sponsor-workspace-prototype` (branch `feat/pan-african-org`)

## Read these first

- Task brief: `.superpowers/sdd/2026-08-20-pan-african-org-site-and-video/task-9-brief.md`
- Prior implementer's report, rounds 1 and 2 appended at the end: `.superpowers/sdd/2026-08-20-pan-african-org-site-and-video/task-9-report.md`

That report is the persistent memory of what was already tried and decided. Read it before you start.

## The situation

This repo hosts a static multi-locale demo. `pan-african-org/en/` holds 13 English pages; `pan-african-org/{fr,es}/` are generated from them plus catalogs in `pan-african-org/i18n/`. Everything currently passes: `org:check` 1852/1852 (100%), 45/45 Playwright, 203/203 unit tests.

Across this task we hunted one defect class: **user-visible English reaching the DOM through JavaScript string literals.** Example of the bug, since fixed:

```
onclick="alert('Re-invited Savanna Freight Partners')"
```

On the French page that pops an English alert. **Seven such leaks were found and fixed** across `entities.html`, `general-report.html`, `jobs-applications.html`, `skill-gap.html`, and `users-management.html`. They are all routed through the pages' `STR` blocks now.

**Every one of those seven was found by a human running a manual grep. Not one was caught by an automated gate.** `org:check` reports 100% honestly — it scans static text nodes, and these literals are not text nodes. The Playwright layout spec never clicks anything.

Four instance-pinned Playwright tests were added, each asserting an exact French string on an exact row of an exact page. None of them would fail if a new literal leaked on a page they do not touch.

## Your job: build the gate that catches the class

Write a **static lint test** — `node:test`, reads files, no browser — over `pan-african-org/en/*.html`.

For every English page, extract every string literal appearing:
- inside an `on*="..."` handler attribute, and
- inside any `alert(` or `confirm(` call within a `<script>` block.

For each literal, assert it falls into exactly one of these buckets:

1. **Not user-facing** — no alphabetic content, or it is a hex colour, a CSS class name, an element id, or a numeric value.
2. **A documented internal key** — from a small explicit allowlist declared in the test file, each entry carrying a one-line comment stating why it never reaches the DOM. Today that is `'suspend'` and `'reject'`, which `openModeration()` uses only for comparisons (verified: they are never assigned to `.textContent` or `.innerHTML`).
3. **A protected proper noun** — present in `pan-african-org/i18n/do-not-translate.json`. Company names and person names live here.
4. **Routed through STR** — the argument is `STR.something` or `fmt(STR.something, ...)` rather than a bare literal.

A literal matching none of these fails the test, naming the **file, line, and the literal**, with a message pointing the reader at the four options.

Note: hex colours reach `changeThemeColor(swatchEl, hexColor)` in `tenant-branding.html` and are only ever assigned to `.style.background` — bucket 1.

## Three requirements

1. **Prove the gate works by watching it fail.** Temporarily reintroduce one of the fixed leaks — the re-invite alert in `entities.html` is cleanest — run the test, confirm it fails and names that literal, then restore the file. Put the failing output in your report. A gate you have not seen fail is not a gate.
2. **There is an uncommitted change already in the working tree**: `'Wanjiru'` was added to `pan-african-org/i18n/do-not-translate.json`. Keep it. Your test reads that list as its proper-noun bucket, which gives the entry a real job. (`'Wanjiru'` is passed as a `{name}` placeholder value at `users-management.html:672`.)
3. **Keep the allowlist small and commented.** If it starts absorbing genuinely user-facing strings, the gate stops being one.

## What not to do

- Do not remove or weaken the four existing instance-pinned Playwright tests. They prove runtime behaviour a static test cannot. This adds a layer.
- Do not touch `pan-african-org/{fr,es}/` by hand — they are generated.
- Do not touch the ministry site: repo root `*.html`, `/fr`, `/es`, or `tutorial-video*/`.
- Do not change the English pages except for the temporary, reverted deliberate-failure check.

## Finish

Run `npm test` and `npx playwright test tests/org-layout.spec.js`. Both must pass. Confirm `git status --porcelain fr/ es/ index.html tutorial-video/` is empty.

Append a round-3 section to `.superpowers/sdd/2026-08-20-pan-african-org-site-and-video/task-9-report.md` covering the test's design, the deliberate-failure evidence with its actual output, the final allowlist with justifications, and how many literals the gate classifies into each bucket on a clean run. Then commit.

Reply with ONLY (under 15 lines): Status, commits (short SHA + subject), a one-line test summary, any concerns, and the report file path.

- design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Rounds 1-2 fixed the seven known leaks by hand, one grep sweep at a time.
`org:check` still reports 100% honestly, because it only ever walked static
text nodes — it has no way to see a string literal sitting inside a JS
event-handler attribute or an `alert()`/`confirm()` call. This round builds
the gate the brief asked for: a static lint test, `node:test`, no browser,
that would have caught all seven leaks the first time and catches the next
one automatically.

### Design

New file: `tests/js-string-literal-gate.test.js`.

**Extraction.** Two passes over each `pan-african-org/en/*.html` file's raw
text:

1. `extractOnAttrLiterals` — regex-matches every `on[a-z]+="..."` attribute
   in the file (this also catches the pages' dynamically-built rows, since
   those are JS template literals that construct `onclick="..."` text
   verbatim — the same textual pattern the round-1/2 leaks were found in).
   Within each attribute's value, a hand-written scanner (`scanLiterals`)
   walks character-by-character to pull out every top-level single-quoted
   string literal.
2. `extractScriptAlertLiterals` — finds every `<script>...</script>` block
   that isn't an external `src="..."` include, locates every `alert(` /
   `confirm(` call inside it by tracking paren depth to the matching `)`,
   and runs the same `scanLiterals` scanner over each call's argument text.

**Why a hand-written scanner instead of `'([^']*)'`.** A naive
non-greedy-quote regex breaks on real markup in this codebase. Two cases
forced the more careful implementation:

- `entities.html:1031`:
  `` onclick="openModeration('suspend', '${row.querySelector('strong').textContent}')" ``
  — the outer literal's `${...}` interpolation contains its OWN nested
  single-quoted string (`'strong'`). A simple `'([^']*)'` regex pairs the
  four quotes wrong (1st-with-2nd, 3rd-with-4th) and extracts two garbage
  fragments instead of the one real literal.
- `entities.html:1009`:
  `` onclick="alert('${fmt(STR.reinvitedName, { name: activeModName })}')" ``
  — same shape: an interpolation whose expression contains braces of its
  own (`{ name: activeModName }`).

`scanLiterals` handles both by tracking brace depth once it sees `${`, and
by consuming (not terminating on) any nested quoted string it meets inside
that interpolation — so the outer literal's true boundary is found
correctly and the interpolation's *entire* expression is preserved intact
inside the returned `value` for classification.

**Classification.** For each extracted literal, `classify()` checks, in
order:

1. **Bucket 4 (STR-routed):** after removing every `${...}` block from the
   literal via `stripInterpolations`, is there any static text left over?
   If not — and the raw literal contains a `STR.xxx` reference — the whole
   literal is a template placeholder like `${STR.statusVerified}` or
   `${fmt(STR.reinvitedName, { name: activeModName })}`. Pass.
2. **Bucket 1 (not user-facing):** with `${...}` blocks stripped, is there
   any alphabetic content left at all? (Handles the fully-dynamic case,
   e.g. `${row.querySelector('strong').textContent}`, which strips to
   nothing and is neither STR-routed nor English text — it's just a live
   DOM read.) Otherwise: does the stripped text match a hex colour
   (`^#[0-9a-fA-F]{3,8}$`), a leading-dot CSS class (`^\.[a-zA-Z][\w-]*$`),
   or a lowercase kebab-case internal token with at least one hyphen
   (`^[a-z][a-z0-9]*(-[a-z0-9]+)+$`, e.g. `invite-modal`, `is-open`,
   `badge-success`, `fmt-monthly`)? Pass.
3. **Bucket 2 (allowlisted key):** exact match against `ALLOWLIST`.
4. **Bucket 3 (protected noun):** exact match against
   `do-not-translate.json`.
5. Otherwise: **fail**, naming the file, line, source (`on*-attribute` vs.
   `alert()-in-script`), the literal itself, and a one-line pointer at the
   four remediation options.

**Why the kebab-case rule requires a hyphen.** The internal comparison keys
`'suspend'` / `'reject'` are single lowercase words with no hyphen — plain
English verbs that could plausibly leak as visible text. If bucket 1's
"looks like an identifier" heuristic matched any bare lowercase word, it
would silently swallow `'suspend'`/`'reject'` without ever exercising the
allowlist, which defeats the point of requiring an explicit, commented
justification for exactly that kind of ambiguous case. Requiring a hyphen
(or a leading dot) keeps bucket 1 restricted to things that are
structurally CSS/DOM-shaped (`invite-modal`, `.sidebar`, `badge-success`)
and forces anything that reads as ordinary English — even a single word —
through bucket 2's explicit, commented allowlist instead.

**Deduplication.** The same literal can be found by both extraction passes
at once: an `onclick="..."` attribute embedded inside a `<script>`
template literal (e.g. `entities.html:1009`) is textually still an
`on*="..."` attribute (caught by pass 1) *and* sits inside an `alert(...)`
call inside a `<script>` block (caught by pass 2). Both passes agree on
the classification, so results are deduped by absolute character offset
before reporting, to avoid listing the same real occurrence twice.

## Fix round 4 of 5 — two false negatives, both fixed and proven

The reviewer confirmed the gate fires (independently injected a fresh leak
in `report-recipients.html`, a page no instance test touches; it failed

allowlist was minimal. But two concrete false negatives were demonstrated
directly against round 3's classifier code — both closed this round.

### Important 1 — `scanLiterals` only recognised `'`

Round 3's `scanLiterals` started a literal only at `text[i] === "'"`.
Fed a `<script>` block containing:

```js
alert("Brand new leak via double quotes");
alert(`Brand new leak via backticks`);
```

`extractScriptAlertLiterals` returned zero literals for both lines — not
unclassified, invisible, and not counted in stats either. This is why the
reviewer's own injected-leak test passed the first time: it happened to
use single quotes, the one style the scanner recognised.

**Fix.** Rewrote `scanLiterals` to recognise all three JS string
delimiters (`'`, `"`, `` ` ``) via a `QUOTE_CHARS` set, matched
consistently as the opening AND closing delimiter for a given literal (so
a `'...'` can't be closed early by a stray `` ` `` or `"`, and vice
versa). `extractOnAttrLiterals` and `extractScriptAlertLiterals` needed no
changes — they already just called `scanLiterals` on extracted text.

### Important 2 — bucket 4 credited a literal to STR by co-location, not by actually being STR-routed

`isPureSTRTemplate` stripped every `${...}` block wholesale (via
`stripInterpolations`, which discards nested quoted strings as it
brace-balances) and then only checked whether the string `"STR."`
appeared anywhere in the *original* raw literal. A hardcoded English
string sitting in the same interpolation's arguments as a real `STR.`
reference was deleted before classification ever inspected it, and the
outer wrapper got waved through as bucket 4 regardless. Demonstrated
input — one variable-substitution away from the real
`entities.html:1009` idiom this task's own round-2 fix introduced:

```js
alert('${fmt(STR.reinvitedName, { name: "Totally Unrouted English Text" })}')
```

Round 3's `classify()` returned `{ bucket: 4 }` for this whole literal;
the nested `"Totally Unrouted English Text"` was never separately
extracted or inspected at all.

**Fix.** `scanLiterals` is now recursive (`scanLiteralsInto`). When it
meets a `${...}` interpolation, it still does a first pass to find the
interpolation's matching `}` (tracking brace depth, skipping over nested
quoted strings so their braces/quotes don't confuse that count) — but it
now *also* recurses into that same interpolation's text with a second,
independent scan, pulling out any string literal nested inside it (of any
of the three delimiter types) as its own top-level entry in the returned
list. That entry gets run through `classify()` on its own merits, exactly
like every other literal — it can no longer be laundered into bucket 4 by
sitting next to a real `STR.foo` reference. The outer wrapper's own
bucket-4/bucket-1 label is now purely informational (whether the shell
itself is "just an STR call" or "just a dynamic DOM read"); correctness
comes from the fact that anything with real static text — nested or not —
is now independently classified and must pass on its own.

**Side effect requiring a new allowlist entry.** Recursion also surfaces
`entities.html:1031`'s `row.querySelector('strong')` — previously the
entire `${row.querySelector('strong').textContent}` wrapper stripped to
empty and passed as bucket 1 without `'strong'` ever being inspected on
its own. Now `'strong'` is extracted as its own literal: a bare lowercase
word with no hyphen, so it does **not** match the kebab-case bucket-1
regex (by design — see round 3's rationale for why bare English-looking
words are excluded from that heuristic and must be justified explicitly).
Added it to `ALLOWLIST` with a comment: it's an HTML tag-name selector
argument to `Element.querySelector()`, never assigned to
`.textContent`/`.innerHTML`. This grows the allowlist from 2 to 3 entries
— still short, still every entry commented and independently verified.

Checked out the round-3-committed file (`git show 6086ef0:tests/js-string-literal-gate.test.js`),

Round 3's second test asserted only `total > 0`. Per the reviewer: "stays
green while coverage silently degrades... precisely what happened with the
quote-style gap." True, and worth being explicit about *why* a
corpus-based stats test structurally cannot catch that particular
regression: the current corpus contains zero double-quoted or backtick JS
literals, so `total` (and every bucket count) is byte-for-byte identical
whether or not the scanner supports those delimiters. No assertion over

That's exactly why the fix for Important 1 had to be a direct, synthetic
test (above), not a stats assertion.

What a stats assertion *can* still usefully catch is a structural collapse
